comments.story_title: Ask HN: Have you taken on debt to fund your startup?
comments.why_zh: Jason Cohen 谈通过年付预付优化 SaaS 现金流。
comments.text_zh: 在澳大利亚，我们的大型商业银行会根据企业的现金流向企业提供无担保贷款。示例资格要求：年营业额至少 7.5 万澳元；作为当前注册企业运营满 1 年以上；你能从会计软件提供 12 个月的企业财务数据。你需要让银行相信你的企业是一台相对可靠且可持续的现金创造机器。示例条款：年利率 9%，最高可借 25 万澳元，无手续费。另一个与融资无关的招数是年付预付技巧。向客户提供“以 X% 折扣注册 12 个月”的方案。如果你能让一部分客户以比如 30% 的折扣预付一年订阅费，那可能真的会大大帮助企业的现金流。编辑：如果你资料里链接的 SaaS 业务就是你这家，那么既然你目前没有向客户提供年付预付方案，你就 MUST 看 Jason Cohen 在 2013 年 MicroConf 演讲“Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business”中关于优化 SaaS 现金流的分享 [VIDEO]
comments.text: In Australia our major commercial banks offer unsecured loans to businesses based upon the business' cash flow. Example eligibility requirements: turnover of at least $75K per year ; have been operating as current registered business for 1 year+ ; you can provide 12 months of business financial data from your accounting software. You'd need to convince the bank that your business is a relatively reliable and sustainable cash generating machine. Example terms: 9% p.a. interest rate, borrow up to $250k, no fees. Another trick you can do, orthogonal to finance, is the annual-prepay trick. Offer the "sign up for 12 months at a X% discount" plan to customers. If you can get some fraction of customers to pay you for a 1 year subscription in advance at e.g. a 30% discount that might really help the business' cash flow. Edit: if your SaaS business is the one linked in your profile then since you are not currently offering your customers an annual prepaid plan then you MUST watch Jason Cohen's talk about optimising SaaS cashflow from his 2013 microconf talk "Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business" [VIDEO]

comments.story_title: Show HN: Csvbox.io – CSV import button for a web app, SaaS or API
comments.why_zh: 推荐 $49/$99/$249 的定价档位，并建议避开低价方案。
comments.text_zh: 定价可以从 $49/$99/$249 这样的档位开始。（这是 Jason Cohen 那场经典又精彩的演讲“Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business”中推荐的：[VIDEO]）处在极低价格点（比如 $9/月）的客户往往流失得很快，而且与直觉相反，他们每个客户带来的客服交互比更高价格点的客户还多。你从他们身上赚到的钱永远不够覆盖获客成本。砍掉便宜档位也能顺便筛掉那些——怎么说呢——比较难缠的客户。
comments.text: A good place to start with pricing is tiers at $49/$99/$249. (As recommended in Jason Cohen’s classic and awesome talk “Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business”: [VIDEO] ) Customers at very low price points (such as $9/month) tend to churn quickly, and, counterintuitively, send more customer support interactions per customer than at higher points. You’ll never earn enough from them to cover your customer acquisition costs. Getting rid of the cheap plan also removes the, shall we say, more difficult customer.

Being a founder is already hella risky, and accepting VC money increases your leverage and your risk, which is just uneconomic for an average individual to do (unless they are already wealthy). Don’t double down on a risky bet. VCs get preferential shares, and they have a lot of different ways of taking control in the clauses of the contracts you sign which disempower you, and in return you get shitty common shares and often lose control for the worst reasons. The majority of founders only make wages[1]. comments.text: There's a MicroConf talk from 2013 that discusses some of general traits of a desirable bootstrapped business: [VIDEO] (Notes here: [LINK] ) Regarding exits, I'd say low technical complexity also helps[1]. Obviously there's a trade-off, and a lot of custom tech also allows you to differentiate. comments.story_title: 1k True Fans (2008)
comments.why_zh: 主张少数高付费客户胜过 1000 个铁杆粉丝。
comments.quote_zh: Jason Cohen 的一场精彩演讲
comments.text_zh: 这个很难给出通用建议，因为你需要发挥自己的个人优势。如果你正试图设计一家 bootstrapped 企业，这是 Jason Cohen 的一场精彩演讲。他甚至提到，与少数高付费客户相比，1000 个铁杆粉丝的目标并不现实：[VIDEO] 不过我很乐意一起头脑风暴。先列几个问题把讨论带起来：有哪 2-3 件事是别人会来找你请教的？对给你发工资的人来说，最关心的 3 个问题是什么？你当前雇主的前 3 大收入来源是什么？其中有多少来自扩展收入（现有客户随时间支付更多），多少来自 new logos？除了人员的全成本（工资、工资税、医疗保险等），你当前雇主最大的支出是什么？跟着钱走！一旦你开始深挖一家公司如何赚钱和花钱，你就会找到用软件增加收入或减少支出的方法。
comments.text: This is tough to give general advice for, because you'll want to tap your personal strengths. Here's a great talk by Jason Cohen, if you're trying to design a bootstrapped business. He even mentions the 1,000 true fans goal as being unrealistic compared to a handful of high-paying customers: [VIDEO] Happy to brainstorm though. Here's a few questions to get the ball rolling: What're 2-3 things that people have come to you to learn? What are the 3 problems that are top-of-mind for the person who signs your paychecks? What are the top 3 sources of revenue for your current employer? How much is from expansion revenue (existing customers paying more over time) vs. new logos? Besides the all-in cost of personnel (salary, payroll taxes, health insurance, etc), what are the top expenses of your current employer? Follow the money! Once you start digging into how a company earns and spends money, you'll find ways to add revenue or reduce spend w/ software.

comments.text: Thanks for reading, Patrick! I'm a big fan of your work, and your Indie Hackers interview was one of the big motivators that sent me down the solo developer path. > You could probably talk to business owners with problems, launch an (appropriately priced; hundreds to thousands of dollars per year) product against those problems, build contingent on getting 10 commits to buy, and be at +/- $100k in 12 to 18 months. Many people with less technical and writing ability have done this in e.g. the MicroConf community. If you want the best paint-by-numbers approach to it I've seen, c.f. [VIDEO] Thanks, I'll check out that video! I hear that advice a lot from people I respect, and I put a lot of effort into that over the past year, but I was never successful. The biggest problem I ran into was that there's this "disconnect problem." I know I'm a competent developer and can build niche solutions to $10k problems, but I don't know which companies have $10k problems. I can guess at it, but they sometimes don't even realize their $10k problem has a software solution. The companies also don't have incentive to talk to me to explore the possibility if I'm just a developer off the street. comments.text_zh: > 我们已经有一个客户在使用平台已完成的部分。他们每月付我们 250 美元。不错！我希望你意识到，你处在少数人才能达到的位置：有人付钱给你，而且还是 250 美元。我不会用平台的“已完成部分”来思考；更多用户会带来洞见，让你知道什么值得实现、什么不值得。已经有一个用户获得了足够价值，愿意每月付你 250 美元。请看看 Gabriel Weinberg（DuckDuckGo 创始人）的短视频，从这个开始（第 10 个，Leaky Bucket）：[LINK] 这是未排序的播放列表：[LINK] 我也推荐他的书《Traction》，书中讲了你可以测试以获得 traction 的若干渠道。你已经证明了有人愿意付费。下一步是让很多人付费。你的第一个用户是怎么来的？他们如何注册、如何付款？是别人替这笔购买/订阅签的单，还是自助服务？你有没有带他们走完流程/做 onboarding？你花了多少成本？他们从哪里来？你怎样才能吸引类似用户（同一行业、同一职能/角色）？这个用户愿意把这个工具推荐给他们的同行网络吗？这个用户会去会议/活动与同行（同角色/职能或相邻）见面吗？针对这个群体做推广会不会有意思？我推荐 David Skok 的资源 “Zero to 100” for High Growth SaaS – A workshop on how to build your Go-to-Market：[LINK] 你处在第 3 步（Prove it can be sold），下一步是“Find repeatable sales m”
comments.text: > We have one client already using our finished parts of the platform. They're paying us $250 monthly. Nice! I hope you realize that you're in a position few attain: someone paying you, and $250 at that. I wouldn't think in terms of the "finished parts" of the platform, more users will bring insights into what's worth implementing and what's not. There's already a user who's getting enough value to pay you $250 monthly. Please watch Gabriel Weinberg's (DuckDuckGo's founder) short videos, starting with this one (Number 10, Leaky Bucket): [LINK] Here's the unordered playlist: [LINK] I also recommend his book, "Traction", in which he goes over several channels you could test to get traction. You proved that you had someone pay. The next step is to have many pay. How did you get your first user? How did they sign-up and how did they pay? Has someone else signed for that purchase/subscription or was it self service? Did you walk them through/onboard them? How much did it cost you? Where did they come from? How can you attract similar users (same sector, same function/role)? Is the user willing to recommend the tool to their network of peers? Does the user go to a conference/events to meet with peers (same role/function or adjacent)? Would it be interesting to target that? comments.text: > The sort of skills that would eventually allow me to run my own company/team/org. These are different things. Running your own company more often than not implies you have started the company, and the skills you need to start and run a company are different in and of themselves, let alone the fact they're different from running a team in an established company/organization where you never think about how the power is still on. In smaller companies and startups, the opportunity to learn is yours if you want it and the incentive to do so is survival. The company is small enough that you can, if you're so inclined, be involved in and learn about everything. I answered a few questions on some topics you might find relevant: [LINK] There are a few replies there about communication and alignment. More ( [LINK] [LINK] ) A FAANG is so large that the acronym is just five letters, and procuring whiteboard markers to them could be the biggest contract another company ever had. What you want is to expand the spectrum of your involvement or "ownership". One way of doing that is to learn to sell into the enterprise. Imagine you are a startup and you want to sell your product to [insert your company]. How would you go about it? It teaches you many things: What problem does it solve? For whom is it a problem? comments.author: authorfly
comments.story_title: WordPress Drama: From the Sidelines
comments.quote_zh: 正确地指出了对自力更生的开发者来说良好的商业基本原则
comments.text_zh: 我不同意 Matt 的做法，但不同意他为什么真的被迫采取行动。很长时间以来都很清楚，WP Engine 创立时就是为了成为利润最大化的商业模式，以填补安全/可靠性缺口，创始人明确表示这就是他进入这个行业的原因：[VIDEO]（注意他在那里没提 Open Source 或价值榨取——他只是在正确地指出对自力更生的开发者来说良好的商业基本原则）。他提到每月 50 或 100 美元比每月 5 或 10 美元好得多——而当你意识到 WP Engine 今天仍多少还在收那个价时，这让人心里不是滋味。说到其中不光彩的部分，在于：A）WP Engine 多年来价格保持不变或有所上涨 B）但 WordPress 变得更安全了，而 WP Engine 过去独有做的很多事情，他们现在不再做了 C）WP Engine 在赞助会议席位和 PR 支出上的投入，显著多于实际贡献。我认为这些事情叠加起来，才是真正促使 Matt 出手的原因：A）意识到最初创始人创办 WP Engine 是为了利润最大化；作为竞争对手，Matt 自然会有一种相对被剥夺感 B）赞助会议、却在 WP Engine 本身不回馈的行为 C）有传闻称 WP Engine 管理层压制/回避参与 Wordpress Core 的工作，Matt 似乎真的相信了这一点（也许确实有几个真正的 WP 工程师联系过他——但我没见过证据）D）
comments.text: I disagree with Matt's actions, but not why he is truly compelled to take action. It's been pretty clear for a long time that WP engine was founded to be a maximally profitable business model to fill in the security/reliability gap, with the founder identifying this as why he went into the business: [VIDEO] (note he doesn't mention Open Source there or extraction of value - he's just rightfuly pointing out good fundamentals of business for bootstrapped developers). He mentions how $50 or $100 a month is much better than $5 or $10 a month - and that leaves a bad taste in your mouth when you realise WP Engine still charges that today, a little. Where this comes to the sleazy part is that: A) WP Engine has kept prices the same or increased over the years B) But WordPress has became more secure and a lot of what WP Engine used to uniquely do they no longer do C) WP Engine contributes significantly more to sponsoring conferences seats, and PR spend, then actual contributions I think the combination of these things is what actually drove Matt to make his move: A) Awareness that the original founder made WP Engine to maximize profit; which Matt naturally feels relatively deprived of as a competitor B) The behavior of sponsoring conferences, but not giving back in WP Engine C) Rumors of suppression/avoiding working on Wordpress Core by WP Engine managemnet, which Matt seems to have genuinely been taken by (perhaps a few true WP engineers did reach out - no evidence that I've seen) D)
